name: French New Wave
summary: Critics turned directors rejected studio polish: lightweight cameras on real Paris streets, available light, small crews, improvised energy, self-aware references to cinema, and editing that breaks continuity on purpose with jump cuts and direct address. The camera is a curious companion, not an invisible narrator, and the film is allowed to admit it is a film. Spontaneity matters more than perfection: passers-by look into the lens, the light changes mid-scene, and the rhythm is nervous and modern.

editing: jump cuts within a continuous take

rules.when: a long conversation in a moving car or on a street
rules.then: keep one continuous following take and remove beats with jump cuts on the same axis and size
rules.why: jump cuts compress time while keeping spontaneity, and they announce the film's freedom from continuity rules

rules.then: consider a look or line to camera, or a freeze frame, instead of a score swell
rules.why: the movement prefers reflexive distance to melodrama; breaking the frame makes the audience think about what they feel

rules.then: shoot with the light that is there (window, street, overcast sky) and accept its changes
rules.why: available light is the visible proof that this is the real city, not a set

name: Korean New Wave Thriller
summary: South Korean genre cinema that mixes crime, horror, satire and black comedy inside a single scene. Night streets are soaked in rain and lit with cold blue-green mixed with sodium orange; foot chases through cramped hillside alleys are shot handheld from close behind the runner, so the audience is lost in the maze with them. Violence is staged in wide, unflinching, often unbroken frames that refuse to cut away. Tone swings without warning from slapstick police incompetence to horror. Class is drawn vertically: the rich live up the hill and the stairs, the poor down in semi-basements, and the camera keeps measuring the climb.

color: muddy rural greens and browns by day
editing: tonal whiplash: comedy cut hard against horror
sound: melancholy strings or ironic upbeat music against violence

rules.then: stage it in a wide or medium-wide held shot, ideally without cutting, and let it run longer than is comfortable
rules.why: refusing to cut away denies the audience the relief of editing, so brutality feels physical and morally weighty rather than exciting

rules.then: go handheld close behind the pursuer at the nape of the neck, with blind corners and dead ends
rules.why: the audience sees only what the runner sees and gets lost in the same maze, which turns the chase into panic

rules.then: allow a beat of awkward comedy (a slip, an absurd argument) right before the worst moment
rules.why: the laugh lowers the audience's guard, so the following horror hits harder and the world feels absurd and real at once

rules.when: characters of different classes share a scene or space
rules.then: stage the difference vertically: stairs, hillsides, basements, windows looking up or down
rules.why: verticality makes class visible as physical position, so status reads in every frame without dialogue

name: Italian Neorealism
summary: Postwar Italian filmmakers took the camera out of destroyed studios into real ruined streets, cast non-professional actors, and told small stories of working people trying to survive: a job, a bicycle, a room. The camera observes at eye level from a respectful distance, often in wide and medium shots that keep people embedded in their surroundings and in crowds. Light is whatever the day provides. Sound was frequently dubbed afterward, which freed the camera to shoot anywhere. The drama is everyday and unresolved, and the dignity of the subjects comes from patience rather than from rhetoric.

rules.then: frame them wide enough to include the street, crowd or ruin around them
rules.why: the movement's argument is that people are shaped by their circumstances; isolating them in close-up would make the story about personality instead of society

rules.then: stay at observational distance and eye level instead of pushing in or swelling the score
rules.why: restraint lets the audience reach the emotion themselves, and it preserves the subjects' dignity

name: German Expressionism
summary: Interior states projected onto the world. Sets are painted and built at impossible angles, streets lean, windows are jagged, and light and shadow are as much a part of the design as the walls: a hard light low or to the side throws enormous shadows of a character ahead of the character himself. Performances are stylized and theatrical with heavy makeup, frames are composed graphically like woodcuts, and iris shots open and close on details. The camera is mostly fixed, so the distortion lives inside the frame. It became the visual ancestor of horror and film noir.

color: black-and-white or monochrome tints (amber, blue, green)
painted shadows and highlights on sets

rules.then: show its shadow on a wall or stair before the figure itself
rules.why: a cast shadow is bigger, more distorted and less specific than the person, so the audience imagines something worse than any actor could be

rules.then: build the madness into the set (leaning walls, oblique doors, painted streaks of light) and keep the camera still
rules.why: a locked frame on a distorted world makes the distortion read as reality rather than as a camera trick

name: Hong Kong Action Cinema
summary: Hong Kong's action cinema turned violence into choreography and melodrama. Martial-arts and wire-work fights are framed wide and full-body so the performers' skill reads, cut on the beat of impacts and sped up with undercranking. In the gangster 'heroic bloodshed' strand, gunfights become ballets: slow motion at the peak of a dive, two pistols firing, doves scattering in a church, a Mexican standoff with guns pressed to faces in tight profile two-shots. Emotion is operatic (loyalty, brotherhood, betrayal), so cross-cut close-ups and freeze frames are used without embarrassment, and neon city nights frame it all.

color: neon blues and reds at night
editing: slow motion at the apex of action
cut on impacts, intercutting multiple speeds
cross-cut close-ups of eyes in standoffs

rules.then: frame full-body and wide enough for both fighters, and cut on the impact beat
rules.why: the performer's skill is the spectacle; wide framing proves it and impact-cutting gives the fight a musical pulse

rules.when: the peak of a gunfight move (a dive, a slide, a two-handed volley)
rules.then: drop into slow motion for that one beat, then snap back to real speed
rules.why: slowing the apex lets the audience savor the grace of the action and turns the hero into an icon before the fury resumes

rules.then: use tight profile two-shots with guns at faces and cross-cut close-ups of eyes
rules.why: the pistols touching skin compress the distance to zero, so the tension is about loyalty and nerve rather than aim

name: Dogme 95
summary: A Danish manifesto that stripped filmmaking to its essentials as a challenge to polished, effects-driven cinema. Its rules: shoot on location only with props found there, use direct sound only, handheld camera only, no special lighting (one lamp on the camera at most), no optical work or filters, no genre or superficial action, set here and now, and no director credit. The result is raw, close, mobile footage on early consumer video, where the camera hunts for faces in real time and the cutting is rough. The drama tends to be emotional crisis among small groups, and the restriction makes it feel unfiltered and intrusive.

editing: cut for performance, not for matching
sound: music only if played in the scene

rules.then: camera is handheld and light is only what is at the location; no added lamps, filters, or non-diegetic music
rules.why: these are the manifesto's vows; following them is the style, and the visible limits make the drama feel unmediated

rules.then: let the operator swing between speakers and listeners in real time rather than covering it with set-ups
rules.why: the camera's searching mirrors the room's panic, and missed moments feel like truth rather than error

name: New Hollywood
summary: A generation of American directors, influenced by European art cinema, took over a collapsing studio system and made personal, morally ambiguous films about antiheroes. Shooting moved to real locations, often grimy cities and highways. Long telephoto zooms surveil characters from across the street, sometimes picking them out of crowds; interiors are dark and naturalistically underexposed, with eyes lost in top-light shadow; warm 1970s film stock has heavy grain. Overlapping dialogue, handheld energy and endings without uplift reflect a country in disillusionment.

editing: slow zooms as the camera's attention
overlapping dialogue held in wide shots

rules.then: shoot from far away on a long lens and slowly zoom in, letting passers-by cross the frame
rules.why: the zoom feels like someone noticing, so the audience becomes an observer or a watcher, which suits the decade's paranoia

rules.then: let them go dark, with a top light that leaves eyes in shadow, and resist fill
rules.why: underexposure makes characters unknowable and the world morally murky

name: Nordic Noir
summary: Crime drama as quiet melancholy. Overcast, desaturated blue-gray light hangs over flat landscapes, minimalist modern architecture and dark forests; detectives are introverted and unglamorous, in practical clothes. The camera is slow and patient, often watching through glass, across empty spaces or from a distance on a long lens, and interiors are lit low with practicals that leave cool pools. Pacing is unhurried and procedural, revealing institutional and social rot behind the tidy welfare-state surface. The mood is withheld emotion: long silences, reflective surfaces, and landscapes that feel cold and indifferent.

color: one warm practical against cool surroundings

rules.when: an investigator thinks, waits or grieves
rules.then: frame them through glass, a doorway or a reflection, holding in silence
rules.why: a barrier between camera and character mirrors the emotional reserve of the genre, so the audience senses feeling the character will not show

rules.then: use a high or aerial wide of the flat landscape, road or bridge with tiny figures or cars
rules.why: the indifferent cold landscape sets the mood of isolation and reminds the audience how small the investigation is
